title: Sonam Kapoor and Anand Ahuja Bought Five London Flats for Their Staff. Their Neighbours Are Furious. The Story Is More Complicated Than That.
excerpt: The Bollywood actress and her entrepreneur husband reportedly acquired £4 million worth of apartments near their Notting Hill mansion to house domestic workers. Local residents are pushing back — and the case touches on everything NRIs find awkward about exporting Indian household culture.
body:
Sonam Kapoor Ahuja and her husband Anand Ahuja — the businessman behind the sneaker brand Bhaane and the streetwear retailer VegNonVeg — are facing an unusually public backlash from their London neighbours.

According to multiple reports, the couple recently purchased five apartments near their Notting Hill mansion, valued at approximately £4 million (₹51.4 crore), allegedly to house their domestic staff. Residents in the area are not happy.

What Happened

Sonam and Anand already own a mansion in one of London's most exclusive postcodes, reportedly valued at around £270 million (₹270 crore according to some Indian reports, though this figure is almost certainly inflated or misreported — properties in Notting Hill typically sell in the £10–50 million range). The couple splits time between London, Mumbai, and Delhi, and are known to travel with a significant household staff.

The five newly acquired flats, located in the same building or nearby, are said to be intended as accommodation for domestic workers — cooks, nannies, drivers, and other household help.

Local residents have reportedly raised complaints, alleging that the properties are being converted into "staff quarters" rather than being used as independent residential units. Some have expressed concern about the impact on community dynamics and property character.

The Cultural Clash

For Indian audiences, maintaining a large domestic staff is unremarkable. It's standard practice in upper-middle-class and wealthy Indian households to have live-in cooks, maids, drivers, and nannies. Exporting this model when moving abroad is common among wealthy NRIs.

But in London — and particularly in a neighbourhood like Notting Hill — the concept of buying multiple apartments specifically to house servants reads very differently. British residential culture generally doesn't accommodate large live-in staff arrangements in the way that Indian homes do, and neighbours may view the arrangement as a commercial or quasi-institutional use of residential property.

The Ahuja side has reportedly stated that the properties were purchased as investments, not specifically as staff housing. But the timing and proximity to their main residence tell a more complicated story.

Why NRIs Are Watching

This story is lighting up NRI WhatsApp groups and social media for a reason that goes beyond celebrity gossip. It touches on a genuine cultural negotiation that many wealthy diaspora families face: how do you maintain the lifestyle infrastructure you're accustomed to in India when the social norms and residential rules of your adopted country don't accommodate it?

It's not just about Sonam Kapoor. It's about any NRI family that's ever tried to explain to a British landlord why they need accommodation for household help, or navigated the awkwardness of having live-in staff in a country where that practice is associated with a very different historical context.

The Optics Problem

The timing isn't great for Sonam either. The revelation comes while she's promoting herself as a global fashion icon and lifestyle influencer. The image of buying up apartments for servants sits uncomfortably next to the carefully curated aesthetic of her Instagram feed — though supporters argue that providing quality housing for domestic workers is actually more ethical than the cramped servant quarters common in Indian households.

Anand Ahuja's business profile adds another layer. As a successful entrepreneur with investments across fashion, retail, and real estate, the apartment purchases could genuinely be investment decisions. But the proximity to their home and the staff-housing reports make the investment narrative a tough sell.

What Happens Next

There's no indication of any legal action — buying property in London is perfectly legal regardless of your intended use, within planning regulations. The dispute is social, not legal.

But for the NRI community in the UK, this story is a mirror. It reflects the unresolved tension between Indian household expectations and Western residential norms — a tension that money can paper over but never fully resolve.
nri_angle: This story hits directly at a tension many NRIs in the UK navigate daily: the collision between Indian domestic household norms (live-in staff, drivers, cooks) and Western residential expectations. For wealthy NRIs in London, the way you set up your household is as culturally loaded as any business decision.
